"**Hey, Slavs**" is a patriotic song dedicated to the Slavs and widely considered to be the Pan-Slavic anthem. It was adapted and adopted as the national anthem of various Slavic-speaking nations, movements and organizations during the late 19th and 20th century.

Its lyrics were first written in 1834 under the title "**Hey, Slovaks**" ("Hej, Slováci") by Samo Tomášik in Prague and it has since served as the anthem of the Pan-Slavic movement, the organizational anthem of the Sokol movement, and the national anthems of the First Slovak Republic, SFR Yugoslavia, and Serbia and Montenegro.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Aitamurto-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3) It was composed to the tune of "Mazurek Dąbrowskiego" from 1797,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-4)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Aitamurto-2) which was adopted as the national anthem of Poland through a process spanning from 1926 to 1927. The Yugoslav variation has a slower tempo, changed a few notes, is more accentuated, and does not repeat the last four lines as it repeats the last two lines.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-5) The composer is unknown, although modern renditions of the song often used a World War II-era arrangement by Oskar Danon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-auto-1)
In Serbo-Croatian, which uses both the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaj's_Latin_alphabet "Gaj's Latin alphabet") and the Cyrillic alphabets, the song had been titled as (in Croatian and in Serbian standard, respectively):
*   _Hej, Slaveni_ or _Hej, Sloveni_ (in Latin)  
*   Хеј, Славени or Хеј, Словени (in Serbo-Croatian Cyrillic)
In Macedonian the song's title is "Ej, Sloveni" (Cyrillic: Еј, Словени), and in Slovene, it is "Hej, Slovani". The original title in Slovak was "Hej, Slováci".

The song was written initially in Czech by the Slovak Lutheran ministerSamuel Tomášik while he was visiting Prague in 1834. He was appalled that German was more commonly heard in the streets of Prague than Czech.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3) He wrote in his diary:
"If mother Prague, the pearl of the Western Slavic world, is to be lost in a German sea, what awaits my dear homeland, Slovakia, which looks to Prague for spiritual nourishment? Burdened by that thought, I remembered the [old Polish song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C4%85browski's_Mazurka "Dąbrowski's Mazurka")_Jeszcze Polska nie zginęła, kiedy my żyjemy_ ("Poland has not yet perished as long as we live."). That familiar melody caused my heart to erupt with a defiant _Hej, Slováci, ešte naša slovenská reč žije_ ("Hey, Slovaks, our Slovak language still lives")... I ran to my room, lit a candle and wrote down three verses into my diary in pencil. The song was finished in a moment." _(Diary of Samuel Tomášik, Sunday, 2 November 1834)_  
Tomášik left the instructions for his song to be performed to the melody of _Dąbrowski's Mazurka_: "It be sung as: _Poland has not yet perished_".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3)
The Pan-Slavic flag from the 1848 Prague Slavic Congress,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-autogenerated1-6) which was also the Yugoslav national flag from 1918 to 1941 and from 1992 to 2006.

He soon altered the lyrics to include all Slavs and "Hey, Slavs" became a widely known rallying song for Slav nationalism and Pan-Slavic sentiment, especially in the West Slavic lands governed by Austria. It was printed in numerous magazines and calendars and sung at political gatherings, becoming an unofficial anthem of the Pan-Slavic movement.
Its popularity continued to increase when it was adopted as the organizational anthem of the Sokol ("falcon") physical education movement,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-7) which was based on Pan-Slavic ideals and active across Austria-Hungary. In 1905, the erection of a monument to the Slovene poet France Prešeren in Ljubljana was celebrated by a large gathering of people singing "Hey, Slavs".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-8) During the First World War, the song was often used by Slavic soldiers from opposite sides of the front line to communicate common nationalist sentiment and prevent bloodshed._[citation needed_]
In Slovakia, the song "Hey, Slovaks" has been considered the unofficial ethnic anthem of the Slovaks throughout its modern history, especially at times of revolution._[citation needed_] Although after the First World War the song "Nad Tatrou sa blýska" became the official Slovak part in the national anthem of Czechoslovakia and then again in 1993 in anthem of independent Slovakia, "Hey, Slovaks" is still considered a "second" national anthem by many (usually more nationalistic) people. In the clerofascistSlovak Republic (1939–45), "Hej, Slováci" was made the state anthem.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-10)

The first appearance of "Hey, Slavs" in Yugoslavia was during the Illyrian movement. Dragutin Rakovac translated the song, naming it "Hey, Illyrians" (Croatian: _Hej, Iliri_). Until the Second World War, the translation did not undergo many changes, except that the Illyrians became Slavs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-bbc-11)
In 1941 the Second World War engulfed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The Axis powersinvaded in early April, and the Yugoslav royal army disintegrated and capitulated in just two and a half weeks. Since the old Yugoslav anthem included references to king and kingdom, the anti-royalist Partisan resistance led by Josip Broz Tito and his Communist party decided to avoid it and opted for "Hey, Slavs" instead. The song was sung at both the first and second sessions of AVNOJ, the legislative body of the resistance, and it gradually became the _de facto_ national anthem of Democratic Federal Yugoslavia (new Yugoslavia)._[citation needed_]
Audio 15Duration: 53 seconds.

The old state anthem was officially abandoned after liberation in 1945, but no new national anthem to replace it was officially adopted. There were several attempts to promote other, more specifically Yugoslav songs as the national anthem, but none gained much public support and "Hey, Slavs" continued to be used unofficially. The search for a better candidate continued up to 1988, while in 1977 the law only named the national anthem as "Hey, Slavs" as a temporary state anthem until a new one was adopted, which never happened._[citation needed_]

"Hey, Slavs" under its Serbo-Croatian title "Hej, Slaveni" was therefore the national anthem of Yugoslavia for a total of 48 years, from 1943 to 1992. With the formal adoption (inauguration) of Amendment IX to the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the song "Hey, Slavs" gained constitutional sanction as the national anthem on November 25, 1988. After 43 years of continued use as the _de facto_ national anthem, the delegates simply brought the law in line with custom.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-12)

Serbia/Yugoslavia never copied the Polish anthem note-for-note, but the rhetorical and musical kinship between their early 19th-century anthems reflects shared political ideas, musical fashions, and the transnational circulation of revolutionary songs in Europe.
Key points

*   Shared revolutionary context: Both Poland’s "Mazurek Dąbrowskiego" (1797) and Serbian patriotic songs emerged during the Napoleonic era and the wave of national-liberation movements. Composers and poets in oppressed or partitioned nations borrowed styles and forms that were effective at rallying émigrés and insurgents.  
*   Mazurka form and march-like rhetoric: The Polish anthem is written as a mazurka-derived patriotic march with a strong, singable melody and military cadence. Early Serbian and South Slavic patriotic songs adopted similar march rhythms, strophic structures, and declamatory phrasing because those elements conveyed determination, collective movement, and fit volunteer armies’ singing traditions.  
*   Cultural transfer via émigré networks and printed songbooks: Polish emigrant circles, military units, and printed patriotic song collections were widely circulated in Europe. Music publishers and traveling musicians spread tunes and templates; composers in Serbia were exposed to these models through Vienna, Budapest, and other cultural hubs where Central European musical idioms blended.  
*   Specific influence rather than literal borrowing: Several Serbian anthems and patriotic songs (early 19th century) show melodic or structural resemblance to Polish models—robust, diatonic melodies, short repeated phrases, and call-and-response or rhetorical lines—rather than direct melodic quotation. The resemblance is stylistic: adoption of anthemic materials and public-song conventions common across Europe.  
*   Political symbolism: Poland’s anthem celebrated a national volunteer tradition and restoration of the nation—messages that resonated with Serbs seeking autonomy from the Ottoman Empire. Emulating the tone and form of a successful national hymn was a deliberate way to place the Serbian cause in the same rhetorical family as other European national movements.
Examples and trajectories

*   "Hej Sloveni" (Hey, Slavs), composed 1834–1838 by Samuel Tomášik and later used as Yugoslavia’s anthem (1943–2006 in various forms), adopted a Slavic-pan-national rhetoric and a hymn-like singable melody rather than directly copying the Polish tune, but its public function and martial rhythm echo the same anthemic repertoire.  
*   Early Serbian revolutionary songs (e.g., those from the First and Second Serbian Uprisings, 1804–1815) were influenced by military marches and folk-derived patriotic strophic songs familiar across Central and Eastern Europe. Exposure to Polish and other national songs via Austrian and Hungarian cultural circulation helped shape their form.
Why this matters
*   The resemblance is evidence of how 19th-century nationalist movements learned from one another: they borrowed forms that worked—simple, memorable melodies; strophic, repeatable texts; and militarized lyrical content—to create cohesion and mobilize support.  
*   Musical similarity does not imply plagiarism but shared genre conventions and transnational exchange. The Polish anthem was a successful prototype for a national-liberation hymn; other emerging nations naturally modeled their patriotic music on that prototype.
Concise summary
Serbian/Yugoslav anthems resemble the Polish anthem because 19th-century nationalist composers borrowed anthemic musical and rhetorical conventions circulating across Europe—march rhythms, singable strophic melodies, and revolutionary rhetoric—rather than literally copying the Polish tune. The Polish anthem functioned as an influential prototype for national mobilization, and its style suited the political aims of Serbian and South Slavic movements.

"**Hey, Slavs**" is a patriotic song dedicated to the Slavs and widely considered to be the Pan-Slavic anthem. It was adapted and adopted as the national anthem of various Slavic-speaking nations, movements and organizations during the late 19th and 20th century.
texts.1:
Its lyrics were first written in 1834 under the title "**Hey, Slovaks**" ("Hej, Slováci") by Samo Tomášik in Prague and it has since served as the anthem of the Pan-Slavic movement, the organizational anthem of the Sokol movement, and the national anthems of the First Slovak Republic, SFR Yugoslavia, and Serbia and Montenegro.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Aitamurto-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3) It was composed to the tune of "Mazurek Dąbrowskiego" from 1797,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-4)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Aitamurto-2) which was adopted as the national anthem of Poland through a process spanning from 1926 to 1927. The Yugoslav variation has a slower tempo, changed a few notes, is more accentuated, and does not repeat the last four lines as it repeats the last two lines.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-5) The composer is unknown, although modern renditions of the song often used a World War II-era arrangement by Oskar Danon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-auto-1)
In Serbo-Croatian, which uses both the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaj's_Latin_alphabet "Gaj's Latin alphabet") and the Cyrillic alphabets, the song had been titled as (in Croatian and in Serbian standard, respectively):
*   _Hej, Slaveni_ or _Hej, Sloveni_ (in Latin)  
*   Хеј, Славени or Хеј, Словени (in Serbo-Croatian Cyrillic)
In Macedonian the song's title is "Ej, Sloveni" (Cyrillic: Еј, Словени), and in Slovene, it is "Hej, Slovani". The original title in Slovak was "Hej, Slováci".

The song was written initially in Czech by the Slovak Lutheran ministerSamuel Tomášik while he was visiting Prague in 1834. He was appalled that German was more commonly heard in the streets of Prague than Czech.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3) He wrote in his diary:
"If mother Prague, the pearl of the Western Slavic world, is to be lost in a German sea, what awaits my dear homeland, Slovakia, which looks to Prague for spiritual nourishment? Burdened by that thought, I remembered the [old Polish song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C4%85browski's_Mazurka "Dąbrowski's Mazurka")_Jeszcze Polska nie zginęła, kiedy my żyjemy_ ("Poland has not yet perished as long as we live."). That familiar melody caused my heart to erupt with a defiant _Hej, Slováci, ešte naša slovenská reč žije_ ("Hey, Slovaks, our Slovak language still lives")... I ran to my room, lit a candle and wrote down three verses into my diary in pencil. The song was finished in a moment." _(Diary of Samuel Tomášik, Sunday, 2 November 1834)_  
Tomášik left the instructions for his song to be performed to the melody of _Dąbrowski's Mazurka_: "It be sung as: _Poland has not yet perished_".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3)

He soon altered the lyrics to include all Slavs and "Hey, Slavs" became a widely known rallying song for Slav nationalism and Pan-Slavic sentiment, especially in the West Slavic lands governed by Austria. It was printed in numerous magazines and calendars and sung at political gatherings, becoming an unofficial anthem of the Pan-Slavic movement.
Its popularity continued to increase when it was adopted as the organizational anthem of the Sokol ("falcon") physical education movement,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-7) which was based on Pan-Slavic ideals and active across Austria-Hungary. In 1905, the erection of a monument to the Slovene poet France Prešeren in Ljubljana was celebrated by a large gathering of people singing "Hey, Slavs".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-8) During the First World War, the song was often used by Slavic soldiers from opposite sides of the front line to communicate common nationalist sentiment and prevent bloodshed._[citation needed_]
In Slovakia, the song "Hey, Slovaks" has been considered the unofficial ethnic anthem of the Slovaks throughout its modern history, especially at times of revolution._[citation needed_] Although after the First World War the song "Nad Tatrou sa blýska" became the official Slovak part in the national anthem of Czechoslovakia and then again in 1993 in anthem of independent Slovakia, "Hey, Slovaks" is still considered a "second" national anthem by many (usually more nationalistic) people. In the clerofascistSlovak Republic (1939–45), "Hej, Slováci" was made the state anthem.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-10)

The first appearance of "Hey, Slavs" in Yugoslavia was during the Illyrian movement. Dragutin Rakovac translated the song, naming it "Hey, Illyrians" (Croatian: _Hej, Iliri_). Until the Second World War, the translation did not undergo many changes, except that the Illyrians became Slavs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-bbc-11)
In 1941 the Second World War engulfed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The Axis powersinvaded in early April, and the Yugoslav royal army disintegrated and capitulated in just two and a half weeks. Since the old Yugoslav anthem included references to king and kingdom, the anti-royalist Partisan resistance led by Josip Broz Tito and his Communist party decided to avoid it and opted for "Hey, Slavs" instead. The song was sung at both the first and second sessions of AVNOJ, the legislative body of the resistance, and it gradually became the _de facto_ national anthem of Democratic Federal Yugoslavia (new Yugoslavia)._[citation needed_]
Audio 15Duration: 53 seconds.

The old state anthem was officially abandoned after liberation in 1945, but no new national anthem to replace it was officially adopted. There were several attempts to promote other, more specifically Yugoslav songs as the national anthem, but none gained much public support and "Hey, Slavs" continued to be used unofficially. The search for a better candidate continued up to 1988, while in 1977 the law only named the national anthem as "Hey, Slavs" as a temporary state anthem until a new one was adopted, which never happened._[citation needed_]

"Hey, Slavs" under its Serbo-Croatian title "Hej, Slaveni" was therefore the national anthem of Yugoslavia for a total of 48 years, from 1943 to 1992. With the formal adoption (inauguration) of Amendment IX to the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the song "Hey, Slavs" gained constitutional sanction as the national anthem on November 25, 1988. After 43 years of continued use as the _de facto_ national anthem, the delegates simply brought the law in line with custom.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-12)

Serbia/Yugoslavia never copied the Polish anthem note-for-note, but the rhetorical and musical kinship between their early 19th-century anthems reflects shared political ideas, musical fashions, and the transnational circulation of revolutionary songs in Europe.

Composers and poets in oppressed or partitioned nations borrowed styles and forms that were effective at rallying émigrés and insurgents.  
*   Mazurka form and march-like rhetoric: The Polish anthem is written as a mazurka-derived patriotic march with a strong, singable melody and military cadence. Early Serbian and South Slavic patriotic songs adopted similar march rhythms, strophic structures, and declamatory phrasing because those elements conveyed determination, collective movement, and fit volunteer armies’ singing traditions.  
*   Cultural transfer via émigré networks and printed songbooks: Polish emigrant circles, military units, and printed patriotic song collections were widely circulated in Europe. Music publishers and traveling musicians spread tunes and templates; composers in Serbia were exposed to these models through Vienna, Budapest, and other cultural hubs where Central European musical idioms blended.  
*   Specific influence rather than literal borrowing: Several Serbian anthems and patriotic songs (early 19th century) show melodic or structural resemblance to Polish models—robust, diatonic melodies, short repeated phrases, and call-and-response or rhetorical lines—rather than direct melodic quotation. The resemblance is stylistic: adoption of anthemic materials and public-song conventions common across Europe.

Emulating the tone and form of a successful national hymn was a deliberate way to place the Serbian cause in the same rhetorical family as other European national movements.

*   The resemblance is evidence of how 19th-century nationalist movements learned from one another: they borrowed forms that worked—simple, memorable melodies; strophic, repeatable texts; and militarized lyrical content—to create cohesion and mobilize support.  
*   Musical similarity does not imply plagiarism but shared genre conventions and transnational exchange. The Polish anthem was a successful prototype for a national-liberation hymn; other emerging nations naturally modeled their patriotic music on that prototype.

"**Hey, Slavs**" is a patriotic song dedicated to the Slavs and widely considered to be the Pan-Slavic anthem. It was adapted and adopted as the national anthem of various Slavic-speaking nations, movements and organizations during the late 19th and 20th century.

Its lyrics were first written in 1834 under the title "**Hey, Slovaks**" ("Hej, Slováci") by Samo Tomášik in Prague and it has since served as the anthem of the Pan-Slavic movement, the organizational anthem of the Sokol movement, and the national anthems of the First Slovak Republic, SFR Yugoslavia, and Serbia and Montenegro.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Aitamurto-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3) It was composed to the tune of "Mazurek Dąbrowskiego" from 1797,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-4)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Aitamurto-2) which was adopted as the national anthem of Poland through a process spanning from 1926 to 1927. The Yugoslav variation has a slower tempo, changed a few notes, is more accentuated, and does not repeat the last four lines as it repeats the last two lines.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-5) The composer is unknown, although modern renditions of the song often used a World War II-era arrangement by Oskar Danon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-auto-1)
In Serbo-Croatian, which uses both the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaj's_Latin_alphabet "Gaj's Latin alphabet") and the Cyrillic alphabets, the song had been titled as (in Croatian and in Serbian standard, respectively):
*   _Hej, Slaveni_ or _Hej, Sloveni_ (in Latin)  
*   Хеј, Славени or Хеј, Словени (in Serbo-Croatian Cyrillic)
In Macedonian the song's title is "Ej, Sloveni" (Cyrillic: Еј, Словени), and in Slovene, it is "Hej, Slovani". The original title in Slovak was "Hej, Slováci".

The song was written initially in Czech by the Slovak Lutheran ministerSamuel Tomášik while he was visiting Prague in 1834. He was appalled that German was more commonly heard in the streets of Prague than Czech.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3) He wrote in his diary:
"If mother Prague, the pearl of the Western Slavic world, is to be lost in a German sea, what awaits my dear homeland, Slovakia, which looks to Prague for spiritual nourishment? Burdened by that thought, I remembered the [old Polish song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C4%85browski's_Mazurka "Dąbrowski's Mazurka")_Jeszcze Polska nie zginęła, kiedy my żyjemy_ ("Poland has not yet perished as long as we live."). That familiar melody caused my heart to erupt with a defiant _Hej, Slováci, ešte naša slovenská reč žije_ ("Hey, Slovaks, our Slovak language still lives")... I ran to my room, lit a candle and wrote down three verses into my diary in pencil. The song was finished in a moment." _(Diary of Samuel Tomášik, Sunday, 2 November 1834)_  
Tomášik left the instructions for his song to be performed to the melody of _Dąbrowski's Mazurka_: "It be sung as: _Poland has not yet perished_".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-Pavkovic-3)

He soon altered the lyrics to include all Slavs and "Hey, Slavs" became a widely known rallying song for Slav nationalism and Pan-Slavic sentiment, especially in the West Slavic lands governed by Austria. It was printed in numerous magazines and calendars and sung at political gatherings, becoming an unofficial anthem of the Pan-Slavic movement.
Its popularity continued to increase when it was adopted as the organizational anthem of the Sokol ("falcon") physical education movement,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-7) which was based on Pan-Slavic ideals and active across Austria-Hungary. In 1905, the erection of a monument to the Slovene poet France Prešeren in Ljubljana was celebrated by a large gathering of people singing "Hey, Slavs".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-8) During the First World War, the song was often used by Slavic soldiers from opposite sides of the front line to communicate common nationalist sentiment and prevent bloodshed._[citation needed_]
In Slovakia, the song "Hey, Slovaks" has been considered the unofficial ethnic anthem of the Slovaks throughout its modern history, especially at times of revolution._[citation needed_] Although after the First World War the song "Nad Tatrou sa blýska" became the official Slovak part in the national anthem of Czechoslovakia and then again in 1993 in anthem of independent Slovakia, "Hey, Slovaks" is still considered a "second" national anthem by many (usually more nationalistic) people. In the clerofascistSlovak Republic (1939–45), "Hej, Slováci" was made the state anthem.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-10)

The first appearance of "Hey, Slavs" in Yugoslavia was during the Illyrian movement. Dragutin Rakovac translated the song, naming it "Hey, Illyrians" (Croatian: _Hej, Iliri_). Until the Second World War, the translation did not undergo many changes, except that the Illyrians became Slavs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-bbc-11)
In 1941 the Second World War engulfed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The Axis powersinvaded in early April, and the Yugoslav royal army disintegrated and capitulated in just two and a half weeks. Since the old Yugoslav anthem included references to king and kingdom, the anti-royalist Partisan resistance led by Josip Broz Tito and his Communist party decided to avoid it and opted for "Hey, Slavs" instead. The song was sung at both the first and second sessions of AVNOJ, the legislative body of the resistance, and it gradually became the _de facto_ national anthem of Democratic Federal Yugoslavia (new Yugoslavia)._[citation needed_]

The old state anthem was officially abandoned after liberation in 1945, but no new national anthem to replace it was officially adopted. There were several attempts to promote other, more specifically Yugoslav songs as the national anthem, but none gained much public support and "Hey, Slavs" continued to be used unofficially. The search for a better candidate continued up to 1988, while in 1977 the law only named the national anthem as "Hey, Slavs" as a temporary state anthem until a new one was adopted, which never happened._[citation needed_]

"Hey, Slavs" under its Serbo-Croatian title "Hej, Slaveni" was therefore the national anthem of Yugoslavia for a total of 48 years, from 1943 to 1992. With the formal adoption (inauguration) of Amendment IX to the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the song "Hey, Slavs" gained constitutional sanction as the national anthem on November 25, 1988. After 43 years of continued use as the _de facto_ national anthem, the delegates simply brought the law in line with custom.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Slavs#cite_note-12)
